\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\title{Two Decades of Water Table Fluctuations\\in a Regulated Peat Bog}
\author{S.~K. Lindholm and R.~Adeyemi}
\date{May 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We analyse twenty years of water table readings, ditch water levels, and
rainfall for a temperate peat bog whose outflow has been regulated since
the mid-2000s. The record shows a gradual summer drawdown interrupted by
two multi-year recovery phases, each tied to changes in sluice management
rather than to rainfall alone. We argue that the summer minimum is
controlled jointly by evapotranspiration demand and by the managed
discharge at the outlet, and we provide a simple water balance model that
reproduces the observed seasonal range with a skill of 0.77 in a
leave-three-years-out validation.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Raised bogs store most of their carbon below the \emp{water table}, and
the depth of that table through the growing season is the single most
important control on whether the peat accumulates or oxidises.
Understanding why regulated bogs dry or rewet on seasonal to decadal
timescales is therefore central to projecting the carbon balance of
managed peatlands over the coming century.

Two families of explanations dominate the literature. Climatic accounts
relate the drawdown to summer temperature and rainfall deficits, which
set the evaporative demand on the peat surface. Management accounts
emphasise the outlet regime, where sluice settings and ditch maintenance
control how quickly storm water is released and how much is held back.
Observational tests that separate the two are scarce, because they
require simultaneous records of water table, outlet discharge, and
weather over many years.

Here we assemble such a record for a mid-sized regulated bog in a
temperate lowland catchment. The mean summer water table fell by 11~cm
over the study period, but the decline was not monotonic: two recovery
phases of several years interrupted the trend, and each followed a
documented change in sluice practice. We use this behaviour to test the
two explanation families and to build a simple water balance model.

\section{Data}
The water table is recorded hourly at eight dipwells between 2004 and
2024, supplemented by fortnightly manual readings during sensor outages.
Ditch levels at the outlet are logged at the same interval, and sluice
openings are taken from the operator's maintenance logbook. Rainfall and
temperature come from a gauge two kilometres from the bog margin,
gap-filled against a regional reanalysis.

Catchment inflow is estimated from a lumped runoff model calibrated on
the neighbouring undrained heathland, and evapotranspiration is computed
with a standard radiation-based formula using the gauged weather. All
series are aggregated to weekly means for the analysis, and gaps shorter
than five days are interpolated linearly.

\section{Methods}
The weekly water balance is written as storage change equals rainfall
minus evapotranspiration minus managed discharge. The managed discharge
is modelled as a linear function of the ditch level above the sluice
sill, with a coefficient that is allowed to change only at documented
maintenance dates. The seasonal minimum $h_{min}$ and the amplitude
$h_{max}_{95}$ are taken from the fitted weekly series.

Model skill is evaluated with the coefficient of determination in a
leave-three-years-out cross-validation over the full record. The two
tunable coefficients are estimated on the training folds only, using a
bounded search over ranges reported for comparable sites. No parameter
is allowed to vary between drawdown and recovery phases, so the
validation tests the water balance structure rather than the fitting.

\section{Results}
The observed water table decomposes into a seasonal cycle of 18--35~cm
and a decadal trend that dominates the total variance. Drawdown phases
in 2006--2010 and 2015--2019 account for most of the net decline, while
the recoveries in 2011--2014 and 2020--2023 restored about one third of
the lost storage.

Three findings emerge from the comparison with the explanation families:
\begin{itemize}
\item climatic forcing reproduces the seasonal cycle but fails to
produce the multi-year recoveries;
\item outlet management reproduces the decadal trend but not the timing
of the summer minima;
\item the combined model reproduces both, with a cross-validated skill
of 0.77.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion}
The recoveries coincide with two periods of reduced sluice openings
rather than with anomalous rainfall, which suggests that managed
discharge modulates the summer minimum strongly enough to reverse the
sign of the trend for several years at a time. This mechanism is absent
from purely climatic accounts and is only partly captured by management
accounts that neglect evapotranspiration demand.

The model developed here is deliberately simple: it has two tunable
coefficients, both constrained within literature ranges, and it can be
implemented in a catchment model at negligible cost. Its main limitation
is the assumption of a single outlet regime per management period, which
is violated during storm sequences when the operator adjusts the sluice
day by day.

\section{Conclusion}
Two decades of observations show that the water table of a regulated bog
is shaped jointly by evaporative demand and by managed discharge. A
simple water balance that combines the two reproduces the observed
record with good skill and offers a tractable way to represent peat
hydrology in catchment models.
\end{document}

\subsection{Data Availability}
All level and rainfall series are deposited at the National Land \& Water Archive under the project page listed in the supplement, together with the processing scripts.
